fields.label: Filled in by
fields.help: your name, so we know whom to ask

fields.label: Date
fields.help: the day you filled it in, as YYYY-MM-DD, e.g. 2026-10-26

fields.label: Notes to us
fields.help: anything we should know: where a value comes from, which values are estimates, what you want to learn from this coupon

fields.label: Test
fields.help: the kind of test: unnotched tension (a plain strip pulled), unnotched compression (a plain strip pushed), open-hole tension (a strip with a hole at its centre, pulled), in-plane shear (a strip of +45 and -45 plies only, pulled), three-point bending (a strip on two supports pushed down at midspan), four-point bending (pushed down at two lines) or plate (a laminate held and loaded on regions you name, stated from the studio); see Definitions, Tests

fields.label: Material code
fields.help: a short code for the material in the coupon's name, capital letters and digits: X840PW in X840PW-UNT-L1; leave blank to reuse the code we already use for this material

fields.label: Layup code
fields.help: a short code for the stacking sequence: L1, L2 and so on; leave blank and we reuse the code of this same stacking sequence or give the next free one

fields.label: Standard
fields.help: the test standard the specimen follows, e.g. ASTM D3039, or none

fields.label: Where the size comes from
fields.help: where the length, width and tabs come from: a standard, a drawing, or your own design

fields.label: Your Abaqus model of this coupon
fields.help: the name of your Abaqus model or job for this coupon, or not built yet

fields.label: Test data
fields.help: measured results we can compare with (a test report or a file name), or none

sections.title: Geometry (mm): the coupon lies with its length along y, the direction it is pulled, pushed or spanned

fields.label: Length (mm)
fields.help: the whole coupon from end to end along the pull, tabs included, e.g. 250; for bending, the span plus the two overhangs

fields.label: Width (mm)
fields.help: across the coupon, e.g. 25

fields.label: Tab length (mm)
fields.help: how much of each end the grip holds, e.g. 56; 0 for no tabs, and then set Grip region to line. Required for the pulled and pushed tests; leave it blank for bending, which has supports instead of grips

sections.title: Bending (three- and four-point bending only; ignored for the other tests)

fields.label: Support span (mm)
fields.help: the distance between the two support lines, e.g. 48; ASTM D7264 takes 32 times the laminate thickness. The coupon lies across the supports with its length along y

fields.label: Overhang (mm)
fields.help: how far the coupon reaches past each support, so that Length = span + 2 overhang; 0 for a coupon that ends at its supports

fields.label: Loading span (mm)
fields.help: four-point bending only: the distance between the two loading noses, centred on the span, e.g. half the support span

sections.title: Open hole (open-hole tension, or a plate with a hole; ignored for the other tests)

fields.label: Hole diameter (mm)
fields.help: the diameter of the hole at the centre of the coupon, e.g. 6; on a plate the hole's ring becomes a region you can hold or load

fields.label: Nodes around the hole
fields.help: how many mesh points sit on the edge of the hole; a multiple of 4, at least 8. More points give a rounder hole and a sharper peak stress

fields.label: Element rings around the hole
fields.help: how many rings of elements surround the hole before the regular mesh starts; more rings give more detail near the hole

fields.label: Ring ratio
fields.help: how far the ringed region reaches from the hole's centre, in hole radii: 2 means a square reaching 2 radii out on each side; it must stay inside the width

fields.label: Ring growth
fields.help: how much thicker each ring is than the one inside it: 1.2 means 20% thicker, so the smallest elements sit at the edge of the hole, where stress changes fastest; 1 keeps every ring the same

fields.label: Ply 1 (bottom)
fields.help: the fibre angle of the bottom ply in degrees, measured from x, which runs across the width: 0 = fibres across the coupon, 90 = fibres along the pull, 45 and -45 diagonal. Then one ply per row upward; leave the rest blank

fields.label: Ply 2
fields.help: the next ply up

fields.label: Symmetric
fields.help: yes: the plies listed are the lower half and are mirrored, so 0, 45, -45, 90 becomes 8 plies; no: the plies listed are the whole stack

fields.label: Ply thickness (mm)
fields.help: the cured thickness of one ply, e.g. 0.127; leave blank only when the library material gives one (its Ply thickness column on the sheet Library materials)

sections.title: Material: pick one from our library, or give your own constants

fields.label: Library material
fields.help: pick a material by its id; the sheet Library materials lists each one with its constants and source, and once you pick one this cell shows its constants

fields.label: Own material: name
fields.help: the material's name as in your Abaqus model, no spaces, e.g. X840-Z60

fields.label: Own material: E1 (MPa)
fields.help: stiffness along the fibres (Young's modulus in direction 1)

fields.label: Own material: E2 (MPa)
fields.help: stiffness across the fibres, in the plane of the ply (direction 2)

fields.label: Own material: G12 (MPa)
fields.help: in-plane shear stiffness (shear modulus in the 1-2 plane)

fields.label: Own material: nu12
fields.help: Poisson's ratio: how much the ply narrows across the fibres when stretched along them, e.g. 0.3; no unit

fields.label: Own material: F1t (MPa)
fields.help: strength along the fibres in tension. Give all five strengths, or none: without them we predict no failure

fields.label: Own material: F1c (MPa)
fields.help: strength along the fibres in compression, as a positive number

fields.label: Own material: F2t (MPa)
fields.help: strength across the fibres in tension

fields.label: Own material: F2c (MPa)
fields.help: strength across the fibres in compression, as a positive number

fields.label: Own material: F6 (MPa)
fields.help: in-plane shear strength

fields.label: Own material: source
fields.help: where these numbers come from: the supplier's datasheet and its date, or a test report. They stay with this coupon and never go into our library

fields.label: G13 (MPa)
fields.help: out-of-plane shear stiffness in the plane of the fibres and the thickness, as in your Abaqus material (Lamina). No measured value? For a tape use G13 = G12 and say so in the notes; see Definitions, Material

fields.label: G23 (MPa)
fields.help: out-of-plane shear stiffness across the fibres and the thickness, as in your Abaqus material (Lamina). No measured value? For a tape use G23 = E2 / 3 and say so in the notes; see Definitions, Material

sections.title: Failure criterion: which first-ply failure criterion we report

fields.label: Failure criterion
fields.help: all: every criterion the material allows (maximum stress and Tsai-Hill, and Tsai-Wu when f12* is given below); or one of them; or none. A criterion needs the material's strengths; see Definitions, First-ply failure

fields.label: Tsai-Wu interaction f12*
fields.help: the normalised interaction term of the Tsai-Wu criterion, a number between -1 and 1, neither included; required for Tsai-Wu; leave it blank otherwise, and Tsai-Wu is not reported

sections.title: Loading: the bottom grip is held, the top grip moves; in bending, the supports hold and the nose moves

fields.label: Loading type
fields.help: displacement: the top grip moves by the value, in mm; force: a total force, in N, pulls or pushes the top grip. Bending takes displacement: the loading nose travels by the value

fields.label: Value (mm or N)
fields.help: the amount as a positive number, e.g. 1 mm or 10000 N; for compression we push, for the other tests we pull; in bending the nose pushes down by this travel

sections.title: Mesh: an element size, or your Abaqus mesh

fields.label: Element size (mm)
fields.help: the size of the small pieces (elements) the coupon is divided into for the calculation, e.g. 2. Smaller is finer: more detail near the grips and a hole, but slower. We put a row of nodes exactly on each tab line

fields.label: Your Abaqus mesh: elements across the width
fields.help: only if you already meshed this coupon in Abaqus: the number of elements across the width. Give this and the next two instead of an element size, and our mesh matches yours node for node

fields.label: Your Abaqus mesh: partition lines (mm)
fields.help: where your partition lines cross the length, measured from the bottom end, comma-separated, e.g. 56, 110, 140, 194

fields.label: Your Abaqus mesh: rows per segment
fields.help: how many rows of elements lie in each segment between those lines, from the bottom, so one more number than there are lines, e.g. 28, 27, 10, 27, 28

sections.title: Grips (ignored for bending, which rests on supports)

fields.label: Grip kind
fields.help: coupling: the gripped nodes at each end are tied to one reference point, held at the bottom and moved at the top, as in your Abaqus models; nodal: the gripped nodes themselves are held or moved

fields.label: Grip region
fields.help: tabs: every node on the tab is held; line: only the row of nodes at each end (use it when Tab length is 0)

sections.title: Names in your Abaqus model (optional: give them and our Abaqus file uses them)

fields.label: Abaqus name: part
fields.help: the part's name; leave all five blank and we use ours

fields.label: Abaqus name: instance
fields.help: the instance's name in the assembly, e.g. Coupon-1

fields.label: Abaqus name: material
fields.help: the material's name under Property, Material

fields.label: Abaqus name: layup
fields.help: the composite layup's name

fields.label: Abaqus name: section set
fields.help: the set the layup is assigned to

how_to: What this form is for. You describe one coupon test; from it we build the model in our engine, solve it, and send back a package: the document, our Abaqus deck of the same coupon, and the audit form on which you compare your Abaqus results with ours.

Fill in the yellow cells only. Rows marked 'required' must be given; the others have a default or may stay blank. Units are mm, MPa and N. Every row says what it means beside it; the sheet Definitions explains each term with an example.

Directions: the coupon lies with its length along y, the direction it is pulled or pushed, and its width along x. Ply angles are measured from x, as in your Abaqus models: 0 = fibres across the coupon, 90 = fibres along the pull.
Layup: one ply per row, bottom ply first, angles in degrees. With Symmetric = yes, the plies you list are the lower half and are mirrored.

Material: either pick one from the sheet Library materials, or give your own constants with their source. Not both. G13 and G23 are needed in both cases, for the shell section of the Abaqus model; take them from your Abaqus material, or estimate them as the sheet Definitions says and write in the notes that they are estimates. If the library material has no strength in a column, we predict no failure; if it has no ply thickness, give one.
Failure criterion: all reports every criterion the material's strengths allow, maximum stress and Tsai-Hill, and Tsai-Wu too when you give its interaction term f12*; or pick one criterion, or none.

Mesh: give an element size and we divide the coupon so that a row of nodes sits on each tab line; or, when you already have an Abaqus model, give its mesh (elements across the width, the partition lines from the bottom, and the rows per segment) so that ours matches it node for node.

Open hole: the hole rows are read only for open-hole tension and for a plate with a hole. Bending: the span, overhang and loading span rows are read only for the two bending tests, which rest on two support lines instead of grips. Loading: give the amount; for compression we apply it as a push, and in bending the nose pushes down by it. A plate lists its supports and loads over named regions instead; it is stated from the studio.

Where we read results: at the centre of the coupon and just past the bottom tab; on an open-hole coupon, beside and above the hole and halfway to the tab. You do not enter these points: we place them from the geometry.
Names: if you give the names of your Abaqus part, instance, material, layup and section set, our deck opens in Abaqus/CAE with them.
Send the file back as it is. If something is missing or inconsistent, we send it back with every problem named.

terms.meaning: A test specimen: a flat strip of the laminate, held at both ends by grips and pulled or pushed along its length.
terms.example: A 250 x 25 mm strip with 56 mm tabs.

terms.meaning: Lay the coupon flat with its length running up the page. x runs across the width from the left edge (x = 0); y runs along the length from the bottom end (y = 0). The coupon is pulled or pushed along y.
terms.example: The centre of a 250 x 25 mm coupon is at x = 12.5, y = 125.

terms.meaning: A tab is the end region a grip holds. The tab line is where the tab ends and the free part of the coupon begins.
terms.example: With 56 mm tabs on a 250 mm coupon the tab lines are at y = 56 and y = 194.

terms.meaning: The free part between the tabs, where the coupon should fail and where results are read.
A plain strip pulled along its length. It gives the laminate's tensile stiffness and strength.
terms.example: ASTM D3039.

terms.meaning: A plain strip pushed along its length. It gives the compressive stiffness and strength. Our model is flat and in-plane, so it does not buckle.
terms.example: ASTM D6641.

terms.meaning: A strip with a hole drilled through its centre, pulled. The hole concentrates the stress at its edge.
terms.example: ASTM D5766: 36 mm wide with a 6 mm hole.

terms.meaning: A strip made of +45 and -45 plies only, pulled. The plies are loaded in shear, which gives the shear stiffness and strength.
terms.example: ASTM D3518. Every ply +45 or -45, as many of each.

terms.meaning: A flat laminate held and loaded on regions you name: an edge, a tab, the ring of a hole, the whole face, or a box you draw on it. Each support says which directions it holds (and a travel, if it moves); each load is a force along a direction spread over its region, or a pressure on an area. Stated from the studio, which draws the regions; the Excel form has no rows for them.
terms.example: A square plate simply supported on its four edges under a pressure.

terms.meaning: A strip resting on two support lines, pushed down at midspan by a loading nose that moves by the value you give. It gives the flexural stiffness and strength; the outer plies carry most of the stress, the bottom ones in tension.
terms.example: ASTM D7264 procedure A: 13 mm wide, span 32 times the thickness.

terms.meaning: A strip on two support lines, pushed down by two loading noses centred on the span. Between the noses the moment is constant, so the failure is not under a nose.
terms.example: ASTM D7264 procedure B: the loading span is half the support span.

terms.meaning: The span is the distance between the support lines; the overhang is what reaches past each support (Length = span + 2 overhang); the loading span is the distance between the two noses of four-point bending.
terms.example: Span 48, overhang 6: a 60 mm coupon.

terms.meaning: One layer of the laminate: fibres in resin, all at one angle.

The direction of a ply's fibres, in degrees, measured from x (across the width), positive counterclockwise when you look down on the coupon. 0 = fibres across the coupon, 90 = fibres along the pull, 45 and -45 diagonal. This is how your Abaqus models are set up: the coupon drawn along y, the layup in the global axes.
terms.example: If you think of 0 as the direction of the pull, add 90 to every angle: 0, 45, -45, 90 becomes 90, -45, 45, 0.

terms.meaning: List the plies from the bottom face up, in the order you would lay them on the tool.
The stack is mirrored about its middle. With Symmetric = yes, list only the lower half.
The cured thickness of one ply.
A material whose constants we hold with their source and page. Pick its id; the sheet Library materials lists each one with its constants, and the row on the form shows the one you picked.
terms.example: im7-8552: IM7/8552 carbon/epoxy tape, NCAMP.

terms.term: Empty cell on the sheet Library materials
terms.meaning: The source does not give that value. With no strength we cannot predict when a ply fails, so we leave failure out; with no ply thickness, give one on the form.
Your own constants, with where they come from. They stay with this coupon and never go into our library.
The ply's own directions: 1 along the fibres, 2 across the fibres in the plane of the ply, 3 through the thickness.
Stiffness (Young's modulus) along the fibres (E1) and across them (E2).
terms.example: IM7/8552 in our library: E1 = 162,096 MPa, E2 = 8,963 MPa.

terms.meaning: In-plane shear stiffness: how the ply resists shear in its own plane.
Poisson's ratio: how much the ply narrows across the fibres when it is stretched along them. No unit.

terms.term: Strengths F1t, F1c, F2t, F2c, F6
terms.meaning: The stress at which a ply fails: along the fibres in tension (F1t) and compression (F1c), across the fibres in tension (F2t) and compression (F2c), and in in-plane shear (F6). Compression as a positive number. Give all five or none.

The rule that says when a ply has failed, from its stresses and strengths. Maximum stress: a ply fails when one stress reaches its strength. Tsai-Hill and Tsai-Wu: the stresses are combined, so no single one governs. All reports every criterion the material's strengths allow.
terms.example: all, our default; or one of maximum stress, tsai-hill, tsai-wu; or none.

terms.meaning: The interaction term of the Tsai-Wu criterion, normalised, between -1 and 1 (neither included). Tsai-Wu needs it; the other criteria do not.
terms.example: Leave it blank and Tsai-Wu is not reported.

terms.meaning: Out-of-plane shear stiffness: G13 in the plane that holds the fibres and the thickness, G23 across the fibres and the thickness. Abaqus needs them for the shell section (its Lamina material asks for them). Our own solver does not use them, so they do not change our results for a thin coupon pulled or pushed.
terms.example: No measured value: for a tape the usual estimate is G13 = G12 and G23 = E2 / 3 (the ply taken as the same in every direction across the fibres, with nu23 = 0.5; MIL-HDBK-17-3F, section 10.2.4.1). For a woven fabric there is no reliable estimate: ask the supplier. Either way, write in the notes which values are estimates.

terms.meaning: Where your own constants come from.
terms.example: The supplier's datasheet and its date, or a test report and its number.

terms.meaning: The top grip moves by a set distance; the bottom grip is held. We report the force it takes.
terms.example: 1 mm.

terms.meaning: A set total force pulls or pushes the top grip; the bottom grip is held. We report how far it moves.
The gripped nodes at each end are tied to one reference point, which moves like a rigid grip: held at the bottom, moved at the top. This is how your Abaqus models grip the coupon.
The gripped nodes are held or moved directly, without a reference point.
tabs: every node on the tab is held. line: only the row of nodes at each end.
terms.example: Use line when Tab length is 0.

terms.meaning: For the calculation the coupon is divided into small four-sided pieces called elements; their corners are the nodes. The stress is worked out in every element. The whole set of elements is the mesh.
terms.example: A 250 x 20 mm coupon with 2 mm elements has 10 across and 125 along: 1,250 elements.

terms.meaning: About how long an element's side is. We divide the width, and each part of the length, into whole numbers of elements of about this size, with a row of nodes exactly on each tab line.
terms.example: 2 mm, our default; 1 mm for a finer check.

terms.meaning: Smaller elements. They show more detail where the stress changes quickly (at the end of a tab, around a hole) and take longer to solve. In the middle of a plain coupon the stress is the same everywhere, so a finer mesh changes nothing there.

If you have meshed this coupon in Abaqus, give its seeds instead of an element size: elements across the width, the partition lines from the bottom, and the rows in each segment. Our mesh is then the same as yours node for node, and the results can be compared element by element.

Nodes around the hole: points on the hole's edge. Element rings: rings of elements around the hole. Ring ratio: how far the ringed region reaches, in hole radii. Ring growth: how much thicker each ring is than the one inside it.
terms.example: Our defaults: 32 nodes, 6 rings, ratio 2, growth 1.2.

terms.meaning: The force the grip needs to make the movement you gave.
The load at which the first ply anywhere in the coupon reaches its strength, by the criterion you chose on the Failure criterion row; given as a fraction of your load, with the place and the ply.
terms.example: 0.93: the first ply fails at 93% of a 1 mm pull.

terms.meaning: At the centre of the coupon and just past the bottom tab; on an open-hole coupon, beside and above the hole and halfway to the tab. We place these points from the geometry; you do not enter them.
Material code, test code and layup code. Test codes: UNT unnotched tension, UNC unnotched compression, OHT open-hole tension, IPS in-plane shear.
terms.example: X840PW-UNT-L1: X840 plain weave, unnotched tension, layup 1.
